Task T1 · The shelf page · November 5, 2026

Three directions for the shelf

The shelf is Trove's home screen, where members browse books and pick one worth a 30-minute conversation. This page sets out who it's for, the feeling it should have, and three ways to build it. All books, names and shelf labels are samples; shelf categories are placeholders until they're decided.

1 · Investigation

Who opens this page, and what they feel

Students

They open a networking app feeling like they're asking for something. They expect to be ignored, worry they have nothing to say, and dread the cold message. Handshake and LinkedIn make them applicants.

The shelf has to show their own book on the same shelf, dressed the same, and let them be curious instead of strategic.

Alumni

They open it braced for asks. Most want to give back, but fear a flood, another profile to keep up, and being treated as a door to a job. Most of what they know isn't on their résumé, and nobody asks about it.

The shelf has to show people, not candidates, and nothing that asks them to perform.

What brings alumni back

Being asked about the specific thing they know, by someone who read their title. A shelf worth browsing for themselves: alumni are readers too, and a student's book about what nineteen-year-olds think is useful to them.

And nothing to maintain: no posts, no counts to check, no inbox pressure. Coming back should feel like stopping by, not catching up.

What the shelf is for

Browsing until one title makes you ask a question, then meeting the person who could answer it. It's neither of the two things networking pages usually are.

2 · The feeling

Curious, unhurried, among equals.

An afternoon in the stacks with nothing assigned, pulling out a book because its title made you wonder. Nobody is watching, nothing is ranked, and the author is a person you could actually go and talk to.

It must never feel like

LinkedIn
Polish, titles, employers, counts. The place you perform.
A dating app
Faces, swiping, judging people at a glance.
A recruiting tool
Filters, pipelines, people sorted into candidates.
A feed
Endless, newest first, loud.
A themed bookshop
Fake wood, leather and quaintness. A gimmick alumni won't take seriously.

Principles

The title is the face
Lead with the title. The first name is small. No photos.
Every book gets the same frame
Same size, same type, color assigned by Trove. Nothing a VP's book can have that a sophomore's can't.
A visit can end
Shelves are finite. No infinite scroll, no "new" or "trending", nothing that ticks.
Library as structure, not costume
Borrow how a library works (shelves, checkout, the Librarian). Skip the wood grain.
One voice recommends
Only the Librarian suggests, and always with the reason a person would give.

Title
Set large; it's the only thing that competes for attention.
First name
Small capitals at the foot, the way a publisher sets the author.
Cloth and ornament
Assigned by Trove from eight colors and four marks. Variety for the eye, no meaning.
Nothing else
No photo, year, job, chapter count or badge.
Idea
The display shelf near a library's entrance, where a few books stand face out. Every book gets a cloth-bound cover that Trove sets in type. The metaphor is strongest here.
Type
Young Serif for titles: round, warm, a little old-fashioned, and still readable at 13px on a phone. Commissioner for everything you operate.
Color
A reading-room green-grey ground. Eight muted cloth colors for covers, assigned by Trove. The only accent is the bottle green of the first cloth.
Best at
It looks like nothing else. Covers give each book a presence, so a sophomore's book stands as tall as anyone's. It is the most likely to make an alumnus stop and look.
Worst at
Fewest books per screen. Long titles get small inside a 2:3 cover. Authors may ask to choose their color, which brings personal branding back in.

Living With an Engineering Degree You Don't Use

Typed first name
Above the red line, where a catalog card puts its heading.
Title on the ruled lines
Reads like it was written down, not designed.
Rod hole
The one detail that says catalog card. Every card is the same 3×5.
Nothing else
No color, no cover art, so there's nothing to compare but the words.
Idea
The card catalog. Each book is a ruled 3×5 card with its title written on the lines; shelves are drawers with label plates. The metaphor shapes the page; there's no art at all.
Type
Newsreader for titles and the Librarian's voice. Courier Prime for typed labels, as on a typewritten catalog card.
Color
Cool card stock and ink blue. The catalog card's red heading line is the only warm note.
Best at
The words carry everything, which is the most literary and the most equal. It's calm, closest to Substack's feel, and the easiest to build.
Worst at
Can feel archival or cold, and students may never have used a card catalog. Less to look at means less pull to come back. Risks reading as a stationery theme.

A closed book on this shelf

What Nineteen-Year-Olds Actually Think of Your AppPriya
Title along the spine
Narrow capitals-and-lowercase, read left to right, never rotated.
First name at the tail
Where a publisher's name sits on a real spine.
Headbands and offset
Thin bands at each end; piles sit a little uneven. Random, never ranked.
Nothing else
A spine has no room for status, which is the point.
Idea
Books lying flat in a pile, spine toward you, so every title reads left to right. A shelf becomes a stack: a list that still looks like books.
Type
Archivo, narrowed, for spines, the way spine lettering is condensed to fit. Newsreader italic for the Librarian, so the one voice that recommends sounds human.
Color
An evening reading lamp: deep blue ground, dusky spine colors, and one warm lamp color kept for the Librarian and the current page.
Best at
Most titles per screen and the fastest to scan. Best on phones by far, and the same spine works for search results.
Worst at
Dark-first can read as an app for late nights rather than a welcoming place. Spines have less personality than covers. A pile has a top, which could read as a ranking.
4 · Side by side

How they compare

A · Face OutB · Catalog CardC · The Stack
MetaphorStrong: you see booksMedium: you see the catalogLight: you see spines
Books per desktop screenAbout 8About 12About 15
Title readabilityGood, smaller on long titlesBestVery good
Feels equalYes, if Trove assigns colorsMost equalYes, if piles are never ranked
On a phoneGood, as a sideways rowFair, cards are bigBest
MemorableMostLeastMiddle
Main riskLow density; color requestsCold, archivalNight-app mood; pile reads as ranking

Build A, Face Out, and borrow C's spine for lists.

A is the one where the shelf looks like nothing else: a row of books you'd want to pick up, all dressed alike, none louder than another. That's the first impression that makes an alumnus stay and a student feel they belong.

Its weakness is density, and C solves it. Use C's spine as the list form for search results, "See the whole shelf" and long lists on phones. Keep B's typed Librarian slip in mind if A's recommendation panel starts to feel like an ad.

5 · For Josef

Questions these designs raise

  1. Student or alum on the cover? The plan leaves a stage marker open (§3). None of these show one, so student and alumni books are indistinguishable. Recommendation: keep it that way on the shelf.
  2. Who picks a book's cover color? A and C assume Trove assigns it. Recommendation: Trove assigns, so covers can't become personal branding.
  3. How is a shelf ordered? These assume a fresh order on each visit, with the Librarian quietly favoring books that get fewer requests (§9.6). Recommendation: yes, and never by popularity or recency.
  4. Dark mode at launch? A and B are light-only, C is dark-only. Recommendation: pick the direction first, then design its other theme.
